summary: Defines MIB objects for managing parallel-printer-like hardware devices using SMIv2. It is a draft standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Gauges for checking the ports that connect a printer to a computer.

questions: what is the parallel printer mib
which snmp objects monitor printer port signals
subtitle: SNMP objects for parallel printer ports: their type and the on/off state of five status signals.

tldr.problem: Devices with parallel printer ports had no standard SNMP objects for describing those ports or watching their control signals.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an SMIv2 MIB module, para, with a port table and input and output signal tables for Centronics-like and Data-Products-like ports.
tldr.outcome: It is a small Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 1318. It covers the physical layer only and has no read-write objects.

today: RFC 1660 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 1318, and the metadata shows no later RFC obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: What the MIB Covers
sections.content:
RFC 1660 defines an extension to the Management Information Base (MIB) for managing Parallel-printer-like hardware devices. It obsoletes RFC 1318 and is a companion to RFC 1659, the RS-232-like MIB, from the same author.

The MIB applies to interface ports that would most probably support the Character MIB. The most common example is a Centronics-like printer port; Data-Products-like parallel links with a similar set of control signals are included. It is mandatory for all systems that have such a hardware port supporting services managed through some other MIB.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a short list of gauges for the plug that connects a printer to a computer, and every machine with such a plug has to offer them.

sections.title: The SNMPv2 Framework Behind It
sections.content:
The module is written for the SNMPv2 Network Management Framework: RFC 1442 defines the SMI used to describe and name objects, STD 17 (RFC 1213) defines MIB-II, RFC 1445 covers administrative and architectural aspects, and RFC 1448 defines the protocol for access to managed objects.

Objects are named by an OBJECT IDENTIFIER and defined with the subset of ASN.1 allowed by the SMI. This module is placed at transmission 34.
sections.plainLanguage: Each gauge has its own unique name in a big shared directory, so a manager can ask for it by name.

sections.title: Layering and the Interface MIB
sections.content:
The MIB is designed for layered use as described in the Interface MIB (RFC 1573). It normally sits in the lowest interface sublayer, the physical layer, serving higher layers such as the Character MIB (RFC 1658).

The RFC admits it is unlikely that a parallel printer port will actually be used as a network interface, which is the intent of the Interface MIB. The MIB is still tied to the Character MIB, which can share hardware interfaces with network operation, and relates to the RS-232 MIB (RFC 1659).

It is relevant for the ifType value para(34) and perhaps others, and requires the conformance groups ifGeneralGroup and ifFixedLengthGroup. The Interface MIB's ifTestTable and ifRcvAddressTable are not relevant.
sections.plainLanguage: This MIB describes only the plug and wire at the bottom. Other MIBs describe what is done with the data on top of it.

sections.title: The Tables
sections.content:
The MIB has one base object, paraNumber (the number of ports regardless of state), and three tables.

  • paraPortTable: one row per port, holding the port index (the same value as ifIndex), the hardware type (other, centronics or dataproducts), and the number of input and output signals the port exposes.
  • paraInSigTable: one row per port and input signal.
  • paraOutSigTable: one row per port and output signal.

The signal tables contain entries only for signals the software can detect (input) or assert (output) and that are useful to observe. All objects in the module are read-only.
sections.plainLanguage: One table lists the printer plugs, and two more list the lights that come in and go out of each plug.

sections.title: Signals
sections.content:
Each signal row is identified by a port and a signal name. The names are the same for input and output: power, online, busy, paperout and fault. A row reports the state (none, on or off) and a counter of how many times the signal has changed from on to off or from off to on.

A manager can therefore see not just whether a printer line is currently busy or reports a fault, but how often it has changed.
sections.plainLanguage: Each light is on or off, and the table also keeps a count of how many times it has flipped.

sections.title: Compliance and Security
sections.content:
The compliance statement makes a single group, paraGroup, mandatory for SNMPv2 entities that have Parallel-printer-like hardware interfaces. That group holds all thirteen objects of the module.

The Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed in the memo.
sections.plainLanguage: If a machine has a printer plug, it must offer all the gauges. The RFC says nothing about security.
